text_blocks.snippet: The pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes is complex and involves both insulin resistance and inadequate insulin secretion. Insulin resistance, where cells don't respond properly to insulin, is often the earliest detectable defect. This, combined with the pancreas's eventual inability to produce enough insulin to compensate, leads to elevated blood glucose levels (hyperglycemia).
snippet_highlighted_words: involves both insulin resistance and inadequate insulin secretion

list.title: Definition:
list.snippet: Insulin resistance is a condition where cells, particularly in muscle, liver, and fat tissue, become less responsive to insulin, impairing their ability to take up glucose from the bloodstream.
Genetic predisposition: Certain genes can increase susceptibility to insulin resistance.
Obesity: Excess body fat, especially abdominal fat, is strongly linked to insulin resistance.
Lifestyle factors: Lack of physical activity and a diet high in processed foods and saturated fats can contribute to insulin resistance.
Inflammation: Chronic inflammation, often associated with obesity, can interfere with insulin signaling pathways.
Ectopic fat: Excess fat stored in organs like the liver (non-alcoholic fatty liver disease) and pancreas can also cause insulin resistance.
Mitochondrial dysfunction: Impaired function of mitochondria, the powerhouses of cells, can reduce glucose uptake and utilization.

list.title: Consequences:
list.snippet: Insulin resistance leads to increased glucose production by the liver (hepatic glucose production) and reduced glucose uptake by muscle and fat cells, resulting in elevated blood glucose levels.

list.title: Initial Compensation:
list.snippet: In the early stages of type 2 diabetes, the pancreas often tries to compensate for insulin resistance by producing more insulin.

list.title: Progressive Decline:
list.snippet: However, over time, the pancreatic beta cells, which produce insulin, become less efficient and may even be lost.
Glucotoxicity and lipotoxicity: Prolonged exposure to high glucose and fatty acid levels can damage and impair beta cell function.
Amyloid deposition: Accumulation of amyloid protein in the pancreas can interfere with insulin secretion.
Beta cell dedifferentiation: Beta cells may lose their specialized function and ability to produce insulin.

list.title: Consequences:
list.snippet: As beta cell function declines, the pancreas is unable to produce enough insulin to overcome insulin resistance, leading to persistent hyperglycemia.

list.title: Incretin effect:
list.snippet: The incretin effect, referring to the stimulation of insulin release by gut hormones after eating, may be impaired in type 2 diabetes.

list.title: Hyperglucagonemia:
list.snippet: Increased levels of glucagon, a hormone that raises blood glucose, may contribute to hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes.

list.title: Increased hepatic glucose production:
list.snippet: The liver may also produce more glucose than normal, contributing to elevated blood sugar levels.

text_blocks.snippet: In summary, type 2 diabetes develops from a combination of insulin resistance and impaired insulin secretion, often influenced by genetic predisposition, obesity, lifestyle factors, and other metabolic abnormalities. This leads to hyperglycemia and, if not managed, can result in various complications.
